subject: bio
title: Immunity
subtitle: Specific and non-specific immunity, antibodies, vaccines and HIV.
concept: The immune system distinguishes self from non-self using antigens; non-specific defences are the first line; specific immunity involves lymphocytes.
B lymphocytes produce antibodies (humoral immunity); T lymphocytes destroy infected cells (cell-mediated immunity).
Vaccines provide active artificial immunity by introducing antigens to stimulate memory cell production without causing disease.

notes.heading: Non-Specific Defences
items: Physical barriers: skin (keratin layer), mucus (traps pathogens), cilia (sweep mucus).
Chemical: lysozyme in tears/saliva; stomach acid (pH 1–2); sebum (lowers skin pH).
Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf pathogens via phagosomes → lysosomes fuse → hydrolytic enzymes digest pathogen.
Inflammation: histamine released by mast cells → vasodilation → more phagocytes to site.

notes.heading: Specific Immunity — Humoral
items: B lymphocytes: each clone has unique surface antibodies complementary to one antigen.
Clonal selection: antigen binds to specific B cell → B cell activated (with T helper cell help) → clonal expansion.
Plasma cells: produce antibodies (>2000/second). Memory B cells: long-lived; rapid secondary response.
Antibody structure: two heavy chains + two light chains; Y-shaped; variable regions form antigen-binding sites (complementary to one antigen); constant regions determine antibody class.

notes.heading: Specific Immunity — Cell-Mediated
items: T helper cells (CD4+): activated by antigen-presenting cells; release cytokines; stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+): destroy cells displaying foreign antigen (infected cells, cancer cells, transplanted tissue).
T regulatory cells: suppress immune response once infection is cleared.

notes.heading: Vaccines and HIV
items: Active immunity: body makes its own antibodies after exposure to antigen (natural: infection; artificial: vaccination).
Passive immunity: antibodies are transferred (natural: maternal IgG across placenta; artificial: injection of antibodies). Fast but short-lived (no memory cells).
HIV: attacks T helper cells (CD4+) → destroys cell-mediated immunity → AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome).
HIV structure: RNA virus with reverse transcriptase; envelope (lipid bilayer with glycoproteins); infects and destroys T helper cells.
Monoclonal antibodies: produced from a single B cell clone; identical antibodies for one specific antigen. Used in: pregnancy tests, cancer therapy (e.g. Herceptin), ELISA diagnostic tests.

definitions.body: A molecule (usually a protein or glycoprotein on cell surfaces) that stimulates an immune response.
A glycoprotein (immunoglobulin) produced by plasma cells that binds specifically to one antigen via its variable region.
The process by which an antigen selects and activates the B or T lymphocyte with a complementary receptor, which then proliferates.
Immunity resulting from the production of antibodies and memory cells by the individual's own immune system following antigen exposure.
Immunity resulting from the transfer of ready-made antibodies into an individual; short-lived as no memory cells are produced.

workedExamples.q: Explain why a secondary immune response is faster and greater than the primary response.

steps.text: On first exposure, antigen activates specific B cells via clonal selection → plasma cells produce antibodies (slow, 1–2 weeks to peak).
Long-lived memory B cells are also produced and persist after the infection clears.
On re-exposure, the large clone of memory cells recognises the antigen immediately → rapid proliferation → high antibody levels within days → pathogen eliminated before symptoms develop.

mistakes: Confusing active and passive immunity — passive involves TRANSFERRED antibodies, no memory cells.
Describing all T cells as 'killing infected cells' — only cytotoxic T cells do this; T helper cells coordinate the response.
Stating vaccines contain weakened bacteria/viruses only — they can also contain inactivated toxins (toxoids), antigens, or mRNA.
tips: HIV destroys T helper cells → impairs BOTH humoral (B cell activation) and cell-mediated responses.
Monoclonal antibodies exam questions often ask about ELISA — antibody binds antigen; enzyme-linked secondary antibody produces colour change.
For active vs passive: active = your own body makes antibodies; passive = given someone else's antibodies.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
flashcards.a: Active: own immune system produces antibodies + memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: antibodies transferred from another source (short-lived, no memory cells).
Antibodies (immunoglobulins) — up to 2000 per second per plasma cell.
HIV infects and destroys T helper cells (CD4+), impairing both humoral and cell-mediated immunity.

flashcards.q: Describe the structure of an antibody.
flashcards.a: Two heavy + two light polypeptide chains; Y-shaped; held by disulfide bonds; variable regions (antigen-binding site) are specific to one antigen; constant regions determine function.
An antigen binds to the B (or T) lymphocyte with the complementary receptor, activating it to proliferate and form a clone of identical cells.

flashcards.q: Name two uses of monoclonal antibodies.
flashcards.a: Pregnancy tests (HCG detection); cancer therapy (e.g. Herceptin); ELISA diagnostic tests; drug targeting (any 2).

questions.exp: Plasma cells (differentiated B cells) produce antibodies at high rates.
In passive immunity, ready-made antibodies are transferred — no memory cells form, so the protection fades as antibodies break down.

questions.q: How does HIV impair the immune response?
questions.exp: HIV targets T helper cells (CD4+); without these, both B cell activation and cytotoxic T cell responses are impaired.

questions.q: What type of immunity does a vaccine provide?
questions.exp: Vaccines introduce antigens artificially to stimulate the individual's own immune response — active artificial immunity.

questions.q: Which cell directly kills virus-infected body cells?
questions.exp: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) recognise and destroy cells displaying foreign antigen on MHC I.

recall: Describe the roles of B and T lymphocytes in immune responses.
Explain the difference between primary and secondary immune responses.
Describe two uses of monoclonal antibodies.
